title: Last Stone Weight
description: Brute force to optimized: re-sorting the whole array after every smash versus a max-heap giving O(log n) access to the two heaviest stones.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of stone weights, repeatedly pick the two heaviest stones and smash them together. If they are equal, both are destroyed; otherwise, the lighter is destroyed and the heavier becomes the difference of the two weights. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.

blocks.text: Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones, smash them (destroying both if equal, or replacing them with their weight difference otherwise), until at most one stone remains.

blocks.title: Analogy: Repeatedly Combining the Two Heaviest Weights on a Scale
blocks.text: Picture a set of weights, and repeatedly taking the two heaviest ones off a scale to combine them (with a heavier one absorbing a lighter one, or both canceling out if equal), until only one weight, or none, remains.
Repeatedly smashing the two heaviest stones eventually leaves a single stone of weight 1.
Before re-sorting the whole array after every smash, notice that only the two LARGEST values are ever needed at each step, exactly what a max-heap provides directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Each round only cares about the two heaviest stones currently remaining, not the full sorted order of every stone.

Observation 2: A max-heap gives O(log n) access to the current largest value, and O(log n) insertion for the new stone (if any) created by a smash.

Observation 3: Repeating this pop-pop-push cycle naturally shrinks the heap by one or two stones each round, terminating once at most one stone remains.

Observation 4: This avoids ever re-sorting the entire remaining array after each individual smash.
This leads to maintaining a max-heap of stone weights, repeatedly popping the two largest, and pushing back their difference if it is nonzero.
Sort the array after every smash, take the two largest, and repeat.

items: Sort the stones in descending order.
Remove the two heaviest, and if they differ, insert their difference back into the array.
Re-sort and repeat until at most one stone remains.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The array is fully re-sorted after every single smash, guaranteeing the next two heaviest are found correctly.
This repeats the sorting cost every round, even though only two elements typically change.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log n), up to n rounds, each with an O(n log n) sort.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: re-sorting the entire array every round is unnecessary; only the two largest values change each time, a max-heap tracks exactly that.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why full re-sorting is wasteful: only two elements are removed, and at most one added, each round, the rest of the order is unaffected.

What tracks the two largest efficiently: a max-heap, giving O(log n) pop and push operations instead of an O(n log n) full sort.

The core idea: build a max-heap once, then repeatedly pop the two largest and push back their difference (if nonzero), each operation O(log n).

Build a max-heap from all the stones. While more than one stone remains, pop the two largest, and if they differ, push their difference back onto the heap. Return the last remaining stone's weight, or 0 if none remain.

A max-heap always exposes the current largest value at its top, and supports removing it (and inserting a new value) in O(log n), exactly matching what each smash operation needs, without ever needing to re-sort the entire remaining collection.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), building the heap once and performing O(n) pop/push operations, each O(log n).
Space: O(n) for the heap.

blocks.text: This is a textbook max-heap application: whenever a problem repeatedly needs "the current largest value(s)" from a shrinking or changing collection, a heap avoids the cost of re-sorting from scratch every time.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid re-sorting every round", think: a max-heap gives the current largest values in O(log n) without a full sort.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared log n) time; the optimized max-heap approach runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a max-heap, repeatedly extracting the two largest values.
Core Idea: maintain stone weights in a max-heap; pop the two largest each round, and push back their difference if nonzero.
Time: O(n squared log n) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized max-heap.
Most Important Observation: only the two largest values matter each round, exactly what a max-heap provides without a full re-sort.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, quick heap application.
One line memory trick: max-heap, pop 2, push the difference.
